title: 8' Wood-Topped Gabion Bench
summary: An 8-foot wire gabion basket filled with stone and topped with 2x4 wood boards — the longer sibling of the 4' gabion bench, with three extra cross braces down its length.

materials.notes: Fabrication suggestions: Darby and Sons (darbywiremesh.com) or Gabion1.com. When ordering custom-cut pieces, ask for the pieces to be cut to size, closed pieces, galvanized after.

materials.item: 2x4 dimensional lumber — western red cedar, Douglas fir, or pressure-treated pine
materials.notes: Cedar: naturally weather/rot resistant, nice red tone, needs no sealant; costs more — ask for 'knotty' (STK) grade. Douglas fir: moderately rot resistant, strong, cheaper than cedar; good if you plan to paint. Pressure-treated: cheapest and rot resistant, but often poor/inconsistent quality, needs 1–4 months of air-drying before painting, not recommended where food is grown. Order 5–10% more than the cut list to allow for variable lumber quality and incorrect cuts.

Angular, hard, inert material that won't break down over time — quarried rock, recycled pavement (concrete/asphalt), or recycled brick/concrete masonry units. Cut logs or other organic material should not be used. Mix of sizes from 2" minimum to 12" maximum; pieces on the exterior face should be larger than 3".

materials.item: Bracing material (for the center supports, below the middle frame pieces)
materials.notes: Either a roll of 14 or 16 gauge smooth galvanized wire, or excess pieces of the 2x2 wire mesh cut in half with bolt cutters (spanning the full width of the basket, at least 2 boxes / 4" tall).

cutList.notes: Gabion bench top + frame sides (2 used as the long frame rails, the rest become the wood top)
Gabion bench frame — end caps and cross braces

tools: 10" or 12" miter saw (or appropriate hand saw)
Impact driver for self-driving exterior wood screws
Grinder (to buff any sharp wire edges)

steps.title: Mark, label and cut the lumber and wire mesh
steps.text:
Mark, label and cut lumber in order of GB-1 to GB-6 to the lengths in the cut list.

Sort your 2x2 wire mesh into equal-sized piles and label them 18-8a (gabion bottom), 18-8b (gabion side, long) and 18-8c (gabion side, short).
imageAlts: Isometric diagram of the GB-1 and GB-2 lumber pieces and the 18-8a, 18-8b and 18-8c wire mesh panels, with lengths and a mesh adjacency diagram.
tips: Label each piece of lumber as you measure and cut it.
Keep a separate pile of lumber for GB-1 and GB-2.
Lightly sanding the cut edges removes splinters and helps with assembly.
Building more than one gabion bench? A stop block on your miter saw keeps every piece the same length.

steps.title: Build the frame
steps.text:
Place two GB-1 and two GB-2 pieces on a flat surface, aligning the edges as shown.

Use the pre-drilling guide at the end of the packet to pre-drill your screw holes, then secure the GB-1 lumber into the GB-2 pieces with an impact driver and 8 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.
imageAlts: Diagram of two long GB-1 rails and two short GB-2 end caps screwed together into a rectangular frame.
tips: Use a carpenter's square to check each corner forms a right angle.

steps.title: Add the cross braces
steps.text:
Place one GB-2 piece in the middle of the frame created in step 2, and secure it with an impact driver and 4 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.

Repeat with two additional GB-2 pieces, placing them equidistant between the middle GB-2 piece and each end GB-2 piece. Secure both with an impact driver and 8 more 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.
imageAlts: Diagram of three additional GB-2 cross braces being added at the middle and quarter points of the long frame.

steps.title: Staple and close up the wire mesh sides
steps.text:
Secure two 18-8c and two 18-8b wire mesh pieces around the GB-2 and GB-1 frame created in step 3, using a hammer and 32 1.5" galvanized cable staples — 2 staples per piece of wire, one side at a time.

Secure the 18-8c and 18-8b pieces together at the corners using hog rings, one hog ring every other opening, with rings at all corners and edges.
imageAlts: Diagram of 18-8c and 18-8b wire mesh panels being stapled around the wood frame and hog-ringed together at the corners.

steps.title: Brace the center
steps.text:
In the center of the gabion basket, below the middle GB-2 piece, add bracing material using one of two options: excess end pieces of 2x2 wire mesh cut in half with bolt cutters, or any excess 2x2 mesh that spans the entire width of the basket (at least 2 boxes, or 4"+, tall).

Secure the middle support piece with hog rings.
imageAlts: Diagram of a wire mesh brace being hog-ringed in place below the center frame piece.

steps.title: Close the bottom panel
steps.text:
Place the 18-8a wire mesh panel on top of the gabion basket secured in step 5 — this becomes the basket's bottom once you flip it in the next step.

Secure it with hog rings on the four sides and the center braces: one hog ring every other mesh opening, and two at each corner. The gabion basket is now ready to transport to the site.
imageAlts: Diagram of the 18-8a wire mesh panel being hog-ringed onto the basket, with a close-up of a corner hog ring securing all three mesh pieces.

steps.title: Set the basket on site
steps.text:
Rotate the gabion basket 180°. Place it on site with a gravel underlay.

Ensure the gabion basket is straight using a level.
imageAlts: Diagram showing the gabion basket rotated and leveled on a gravel bed.
tips: If it's next to other gabions, use string and line levels to keep the row straight.

steps.title: Fill the basket
steps.text:
Place the gabion in its location per your park's design. Apply gravel underneath to fine-tune adjustments.

Starting with the largest, flattest pieces of gabion fill you have, begin filling the gabion starting at the edges, and continue until you've built up the sides.

Fill the frame with leftover gabion fill until it's level with the top of the wood edge.
imageAlts: Diagram and reference photos of a gabion basket being filled with stone, starting with large flat pieces along the edges.
tips: Place fill carefully to avoid warping the basket, and make sure all gaps are filled for stability.
See your Create workbook, phase four, for more on this step.

steps.title: Add the end boards of the wood top
steps.text: Place two GB-1 pieces on top of the frame created in step 3, using the pre-drilling guide at the end of the packet to pre-drill the wood. Secure the two end boards first with an impact driver and 12 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws, keeping the edge flush with the wood below.
imageAlts: Diagram of the first two GB-1 top boards being screwed flush onto each end of the filled gabion basket.
tips: Pre-drilling at this step helps the screws not split the boards.

steps.title: Finish the wood top and sand
steps.text:
Equally space the other 3 boards between the two end boards. Secure the GB-1 lumber with an impact driver and 20 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.

Lightly sand the rough edges of the gabion bench, and make sure there are no sharp edges of gabion wire — buff with a grinder if any are too sharp.
imageAlts: Diagram of the remaining GB-1 wood top boards being spaced equally and screwed onto the filled gabion basket.
tips: Keep all screws a thumb's width from the edge of the wood.

steps.title: Pre-drilling hole guide (template)
steps.text:
Cut out the pre-drilling hole guide along the dotted lines. When drilling, align the edge of the template with the outside edge of the lumber before pre-drilling.

Not all holes are used — not all patterns use the template. Use the assembly steps above for your hole guide. Keep all holes about a thumb's width from the edge (about 1"), even holes that don't use this template.
imageAlts: A printable pre-drilling hole guide template with five marked hole positions and cut lines, plus a close-up showing hole spacing from the board edge.

finishing: Exterior wood treatment can prolong the life of your park elements, but it isn't necessary — these pieces are built to be low-cost, durable and easy to build by design, so it may be more practical to just let the next generation rebuild them when the time comes. If you do want to stain, paint or seal the wood top, see the finish resources below.
safety: These are DIY recommendations only — tailor the material, assembly and construction to your own project and site.
Building this assumes some working knowledge of hand and power tools, hardware, fasteners, lumber and basic assembly technique.
Before using any power equipment, review and follow the manufacturer's safety requirements, and don't let anyone use power tools who hasn't done the same.
You (the owner) are responsible for any building and safety codes, permits and regulatory approvals this needs.
Clear the site of trash, hazards and unwanted structures first, and identify any utilities that could interfere before you dig.
Everyone helping build should sign a volunteer waiver.
Cut wire mesh and gabion fill can leave sharp edges — wear gloves and safety goggles, and buff any sharp wire with a grinder.
